newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Handover a yawn for HK gold, China sales beckon.
newsitem.headline: Handover a yawn for HK gold, China sales beckon.

text.p: Hong Kong's handover to China raised only a yawn on Tuesday in the local gold market, a traditional sanctury for money in troubled times, but long-term sales to the huge Chinese bullion market glitter, dealers said. "Gauging confidence levels, things are quite stable. I don't think there will any panic buying," said Emily Li, Hong Kong and South China manager for the World Gold Council, an industry promotional group.
Gold has in the past been a safe haven during jittery periods. Uncertainty over Hong Kong's future in the middle of 1983 boosted local gold prices to HK$4,750 (US$614) per tael bar.

Fourteen years later, with Hong Kong's return to China just days away, gold is dragging its feet at HK$3,146 per tael (1.2 ounces) as booming stock and property markets lure investors' capital away for more lucrative returns.
Hong Kong's handover will boost gold buying, however, as tourists snap up gold souvenir ornaments and central banks issue commemorative gold coins, Li said.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the territory's de facto central bank, used 34,500 ounces of imported Canadian gold, worth nearly US$12 million, to issue 1997 commemorative coins, she said.
The People's Bank of China, China's central bank, will follow suit and soon release coins for sale into the Hong Kong market weighing a total of 7,000 ounces of gold, she said.
Hong Kong's gold-buying habits are now more closely entwined with international markets, seasonal demand fluctuations, and of course, with China.

"The (tael) exchange is usually more active in the afternoon when the London market opens and arbitrage starts," said Herbert Tsang, assistant manager at Hong Kong's Chinese Gold and Silver Exchange Society.
Traders arbitrage, or trade on the differences in prices, between local gold quoted in Hong Kong dollars per tael and spot London gold quoted in U.S. dollars per ounce.
In Tuesday's morning session, gold traders paced the exchange floor, yawned and read local papers to pass the time, interrupted only occasionally by a ringing telephone and a buy or sell order.
World gold prices have been overshadowed this year by continued rumours of central bank sales.
Low prices earlier this year swelled gold imports into Hong Kong just before the Chinese New Year in early February, a traditional season for strong demand, Li said.

According to figures from the colony's Census and Statistics Department, Hong Kong's gold imports for the first quarter of 1997 totalled 119.12 tonnes, up from 39.49 tonnes in the same period last year.

"I think the picture looks optimistic (for the rest of 1997). After the handover, we expect more tourists in Hong Kong, and these people will be a major source of purchases for gold, which will be beneficial to Hong Kong's market," Li said.

And while Hong Kong's gold market structure is not destined to change for 50 years, as decreed by the Basic Law, the territory will play a more important role in helping China to deregulate its gold market, Li said.
China is one of the world's top gold markets, purchasing over 200 tonnes of the precious metal a year.

Raymond Chan Fat-chu, head of Hong Kong's Chinese Gold and Silver Exchange Society, said earlier this month during a visit to Shanghai that once the Chinese market opened, unlikely for another couple of years, the exchange would provide a hedging and arbitraging opportunity by quoting prices in yuan.
"So there will be three-way hedging, yuan-per-gram in Shanghai, U.S. dollars in London/New York and Hong Kong dollars in Hong Kong," he said.
The exchange also promots itself in China, and has recently acquired a member from Hong Kong's neighbour, assistant manager Tsang said.
"We will definitely continue in this direction."
